articles.title: Vumedi Raises $140M Series B, Oakland Health Tech
articles.snippet: Vumedi Raises $140M Series B, Oakland Health Tech Hoodline
articles.text:
555 12th St. — Oakland Street Scene
Google Street View
An Oakland health-tech company has raised $140 million in a new funding round. Vumedi, which builds an AI-powered learning platform for physicians, has raised $140 million in Series B funding, with plans to pour the money into talent, research and development, product development and outreach as it expands its clinical learning tools.
The investment came from Oak HC/FT, according to FinSMEs , which reported the round. Vumedi is led by founder and CEO Roman Giverts, and the company describes its platform as a tool that connects clinicians with specialists and peers so they can learn procedures, evaluate treatments and navigate complex cases, the outlet reports.
What the Platform Actually Does
At the center of Vumedi's pitch is scale paired with AI. The platform uses artificial intelligence to turn more than 100,000 physician-led videos and nearly 5,000 podcast episodes, spanning more than 21 medical specialties, into what the company calls an on-demand clinical resource, per the same report. Rather than leaving clinicians to sift through hours of footage, the system synthesizes multiple expert perspectives and links directly to time-stamped segments within videos.
The company says its platform now serves more than 150,000 NPI-verified clinicians and generated over 56 million minutes of learning over the past 12 months. Back in a 2018 interview, Giverts described Vumedi's mission as helping physicians make the best care decisions through what he called unbiased video education in an interview with MPO-mag.com . That same article reported the platform then had roughly 250,000 physician users and 20,000 videos contributed by more than 5,000 healthcare organizations and professionals, including partnerships with 150 hospitals and conferences such as Cleveland Clinic, Mayo Clinic and Johns Hopkins.
Funding Figures Don't All Line Up
Not every account of Vumedi's fundraising history tells the same story. A snippet from 01net referenced a $104 million investment from Oak HC/FT, though it's unclear from that report whether it describes the same financing as the newly reported $140 million round or a separate transaction. Separately, CB Insights lists Vumedi's most recent funding round as a $79.98 million Series B dated May 22, 2025, and puts the company's total raised at $82.08 million across four rounds. The available reporting does not reconcile these differing figures with the $140 million sum reported this week.
Part of a Broader AI Health-Tech Wave
Vumedi's raise lands amid a broader uptick in digital-health investment. Companies in the sector raised $7.4 billion in the first half of 2026, up roughly $1 billion from the same period in 2025, according to Fierce Healthcare . The outlet counted 244 completed deals in that window, with $4.2 billion invested in the first quarter and $3.2 billion in the second.
A notable share of that capital came in the form of megadeals. Nineteen companies raised 20 financings of at least $100 million in the first half of 2026, representing 45 percent of all capital invested, Fierce Healthcare reported, citing deals that included AI radiology company Aidoc's $150 million raise. Clinical-reference platform OpenEvidence, a comparable player in physician-facing AI tools, announced its own $210 million Series B at a $3.5 billion valuation in mid-2025, co-led by Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins with Sequoia Capital, Coatue, Conviction and Thrive also participa

Zacua Ventures Raises $135 Million to Invest in AI, Robotics and Industrial Technology
Published on: 11 November، 2026
Zacua Ventures
Zacua Ventures closes its $135 million Fund II to back Physical AI, construction robotics, industrial technology, energy, manufacturing and infrastructure startups.
The next major opportunity in artificial intelligence may not be confined to software applications or foundation models.
Increasingly, investors are looking toward technologies that can transform the physical economy, from construction sites and cement factories to energy networks, manufacturing facilities and data centers.
Zacua Ventures is positioning itself at the center of this shift, closing its second fund at $135 million to expand investments beyond construction technology into a broader range of Physical Industries, including robotics, manufacturing, energy, mining and critical infrastructure.
$135 Million to Back Technologies Building the Physical Economy
Zacua Ventures closed Fund II at $135 million, more than doubling its $56 million debut fund and exceeding its fundraising target by 35%.
The raise reflects growing investor interest in technology applied to capital-intensive industries that have historically attracted less venture capital than software and digital platforms.
The firm’s investment thesis is built around a simple premise: construction, energy, manufacturing and mining are not merely facing productivity challenges.
They need fundamental operational transformation through AI, robotics, data and advanced technologies.
AI Is Moving From Digital Applications to Physical Industries
Zacua’s strategy extends beyond conventional AI tools, targeting companies that deploy technology directly into industrial and field operations.
Its investments include autonomous construction robots, AI platforms that identify project risks before construction begins, and technologies designed to reduce emissions from cement production.
These businesses are becoming increasingly relevant as industries face labor shortages, aging workforces, complex operational processes and growing demand for AI infrastructure.
The opportunity is not simply to automate existing workflows, but to redesign how physical industries operate.
Why Venture Capital Is Turning Toward Physical Industries
Construction, energy, manufacturing and mining represent enormous markets with persistent productivity gaps and substantial infrastructure requirements.
McKinsey estimates that global infrastructure investment needs will reach $106 trillion through 2040, while Gartner projects data-center power demand could reach 290 gigawatts by 2030.
These requirements create opportunities for startups developing technologies that improve industrial productivity, reduce operating costs and reshape supply chains.
However, investing in physical industries is fundamentally different from funding software companies. Technologies must be tested in real operating environments, integrated into existing equipment and workflows, and demonstrate measurable economic value before they can scale.
From Construction Robotics to Low-Carbon Cement
Zacua’s early Fund II investments illustrate the breadth of its strategy.
Origin Robotics develops autonomous robots capable of finishing interior walls, while CURA Climate is working to electrify cement production and reduce emissions by up to 85% through its pilot technology.

Zacua Ventures raises $135 million to invest in robotics, physical AI and industrial technology
November 15, 2026 by Sam Francis
Venture capital firm Zacua Ventures has closed its second investment fund at $135 million, more than doubling the size of its original $56 million fund as it expands its focus on robotics, physical AI and technologies for industrial applications.
The San Francisco-based firm says Fund II was 35 percent oversubscribed, attracting commitments from more than 30 corporate and institutional investors across over 20 countries.
Originally focused on construction technology, Zacua is broadening its investment strategy to include manufacturing, energy, mining, infrastructure and other sectors it collectively describes as the “Physical Industries”.
The firm believes these sectors offer substantial opportunities for technologies that combine robotics, artificial intelligence and software with practical industrial expertise.
Vivin Hegde, founding partner at Zacua Ventures, says: “The industries that underpin modern life are entering a forced transformation cycle. Housing is out of reach. Energy grids are under pressure. Workforces are aging out. The AI infrastructure buildout is placing even greater demands on the industries already struggling to keep pace.
“These are not isolated problems; they’re converging across the Physical Industries, a category venture capital has largely overlooked. We built Zacua in construction because we saw these challenges firsthand. Fund II takes what we learned there and applies it to the broader physical world.”
Building on construction robotics investments
Zacua has already invested in 34 early-stage companies across 11 markets, with several investments demonstrating its interest in industrial automation.
Among its portfolio companies is Gravis Robotics, an ETH Zurich spinout developing physical AI for autonomous construction equipment. The company raised $200 million in Series A funding from SoftBank earlier this year, reaching a reported valuation of $1 billion.
Another investment is Origin Robotics, whose OG1 robot autonomously finishes interior walls. The company emerged from stealth with $20 million in seed and Series A financing, with Zacua leading the latter round.
Other investments include Flexnode, which develops modular data centers, and CURA Climate, which is working on technologies to reduce emissions from cement production.
Zacua’s first exit came earlier this year when construction risk-management software company Document Crunch was acquired by Trimble.
Expanding industrial investment
Fund II’s investors include Volvo Group Venture Capital, Holcim Maqer Ventures, Hilti Venture, Trimble Ventures, Acciona, DPR Construction, Mortenson and Dubai Future District Fund.
The firm says its corporate investor network provides portfolio companies with access to industrial customers, technical expertise and opportunities to test emerging technologies in operational environments.
Juan Nieto, founding partner at Zacua Ventures, says: “Fund I proved that our model works in one of the most complex and consequential industries in the world.
“Fund II allows us to take that same playbook much further. We are not changing what we do. We are applying the same early-stage conviction, founder-first philosophy and industry network across the broader Physical Industries.”

articles.snippet: Modular Data Center Startup Mavria Raises $130M, but Grid Hookups Remain Unproven Tech Times
articles.text:
By
Shannon Harwood
Published: Nov 10 2026, 2:10 AM EST
Share on Facebook
Share on Twitter
Share on LinkedIn
Share on Reddit
Share on Flipboard Share on WhatsApp
Mavria
Mavria, a data center startup whose founders include former Energy Department officials, announced Monday that it raised $130 million at a $1 billion valuation to build data centers in a factory. The company was founded in June 2026 , according to co-founder Seth Cohen, and its first unit, Terrain 01, is being built in Houston .
Terrain comes in 5 MW units, according to Dealroom , which cites the Wall Street Journal's reporting. Mavria's own announcement gives no capacity figure , and the company has not named customers or published capacity, pricing or delivery timelines.
For the frontier AI labs, cloud providers and data center developers that Mavria targets, the open question is power, not factory speed. DatacenterDynamics reported that Mavria says Terrain can bypass grid delays by plugging into local distribution lines to soak up excess capacity, but the company's announcement makes no grid connection claim . That makes size the number to watch in Texas, where Senate Bill 6 covers loads of at least 75 megawatts at a single site: one 5 MW block is about 7% of that line, while a 100 MW campus would need 20 blocks.
How Terrain Packs Power, Cooling and Compute Into One 5 MW Block
Mavria says Terrain replaces on-site custom construction with factory-based repeatable manufacturing . Customers' compute runs inside it, and the company says it supplies infrastructure without operating a cloud or selling compute .
HuggingNews reports that the units use direct liquid cooling and integrated power distribution for customer-owned compute. Mavria's announcement mentions neither the liquid cooling nor the block size.
Liquid cooling matters at this size because AI racks outrun air. Wikipedia's computer-cooling entry puts air cooling up to 23 kW per rack, while NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack draws 190 to 230 kW , according to earlier TechTimes reporting. At those figures, 5 MW supports roughly 22 to 26 such racks before cooling and power-conversion overhead, and Mavria has not said which hardware Terrain targets.
Factory integration removes on-site assembly work, not the utility connection. NVIDIA's DSX POD moves cabling, power distribution and cooling piping into a factory, shortening connection time from roughly six months to 14 days , yet the pod still arrives at a prepared site that must already have high-voltage power , a coolant loop and a network handoff. Dealroom likewise notes that factory production cannot by itself solve power availability or site-connection delays.
The tradeoff is standardization. Mavria says Terrain should bring more predictable delivery and lower costs , but it has published no pricing , so the benefit remains a claim.

articles.title: Mavria Raises $130M to Date at a $1B Valuation to Build AI Data Centers in a Factory
articles.snippet: Mavria Raises $130M to Date at a $1B Valuation to Build AI Data Centers in a Factory Wowtale
articles.text:
Mavria, a startup that wants to build AI data centers in a factory instead of one custom project at a time, has come out of stealth with $130 million raised to date across pre-seed and seed rounds.
Its latest round values the company at $1 billion. Paradigm led it, with participation from AMP PBC, Liquid 2, Critical Frontier and Dream Ventures.
Mavria calls itself “the industrial platform behind American AI.” In an introduction published November 9, co-founder and CEO Adam Blake argued that the AI race is moving from the lab into the physical world. Intelligence needs data centers, data centers need power, and power needs factories, equipment, supply chains and skilled workers, yet much of that infrastructure is still built one custom project at a time on timelines measured in years. America’s labs and clouds have extraordinary ambitions for compute, he wrote, but not the industrial capability to match.
Mavria’s answer is “infrastructure as a product.” It wants to bring engineering, manufacturing, supply chains and capital together so that every project makes it better at delivering the next. Its first product is Terrain, a factory-built data center platform meant to bring compute online faster, with more predictable delivery and lower costs, by replacing custom field construction with repeatable manufacturing. Mavria is building it for frontier labs, cloud providers and data center developers, and says Terrain 01 is in production in Houston now. Press reports describe the platform as 5-megawatt blocks in which power, cooling, controls and IT pods are designed, integrated and tested as one system before shipping, and the Wall Street Journal described it as modular data centers that can be moved by truck.
The founders worked together at the U.S. Department of Energy, where they saw how unprepared American infrastructure is for what is coming. Blake built one of the largest commercial solar companies in the U.S. and sold a software business to Vista Equity Partners. Nick Poradek is an engineer who sold his last company to Liberty Energy and then helped build Liberty’s manufacturing platform. Seth Cohen started as a lawyer at Kirkland and ended up at the center of the effort to restart American nuclear power. The rest of the team has run utilities, led a modular LNG manufacturer with more than a thousand employees, developed major energy projects and scaled technology companies.
“The next decade will show whether America can build at anything close to the pace its AI companies are moving,” Blake wrote. “We’re building Mavria because we don’t want the answer to be no.” The capital will go toward securing critical supply chains, scaling manufacturing and growing the team. Mavria is starting with data centers but says its ambition extends across the physical infrastructure AI depends on, and it is hiring across engineering, manufacturing and operations.
Plenty is still unverified. Mavria did not say how much of the $130 million came in the latest round. Some outlets reported a $100 million round, and a filing with the SEC reportedly shows $75 million sold after a first sale in mid-October. Capacity per unit, pricing, delivery times and customer names have not been disclosed. At least one outlet reported the first facility is not yet running, with testing due in early 2027, which differs from the company’s account. Woodlands startup Mavria raises $130M to mass-produce AI data centers
John Egan
Nov 16, 2026, 11:30 am
Adam Blake, Nick Poradek and Seth Cohen founded Mavria this spring. Photo courtesy of Mavria
The Woodlands-based Mavria , which mass-produces factory-built modular AI data centers, just emerged from stealth mode with $130 million in funding at a $1 billion valuation.
Mavria raised the money in pre-seed and seed rounds led by Paradigm, an investment firm that concentrates on early-stage startups developing “pioneer” technology. Participants in the funding rounds include AMP PBC, Critical Frontier, Dream Ventures and Liquid 2 Ventures, co-founded by former NFL quarterback Joe Montana.
The company’s inaugural product, Terrain, is a prefabricated data center designed for AI labs, cloud computing providers and data center developers. Mavria says its platform avoids ground-up construction, delivering infrastructure more quickly and at a lower cost.
Mavria tells the Wall Street Journal that the first Terrain unit is being built at a Houston-area factory. The 5-megawatt Terrain system features power distribution, direct liquid cooling, controls and server racks.
“America sets the pace at the intelligence frontier. But the race is moving from the lab into the physical world,” Adam Blake, co-founder and CEO of Mavria, wrote in a blog post .
“Intelligence needs data centers. Data centers need power. Power needs factories, equipment, supply chains, and skilled workers, but much of that infrastructure is still built one custom project at a time, on timelines measured in years.”
Blake and Mavria’s two other co-founders, Nick Poradek and Seth Cohen, most recently worked at the U.S. Department of Energy. There, they focused on reforming the nuclear power sector.
From start to finish, it can take roughly three to six years to build a data center at an estimated cost of $10 million to $37 million per megawatt. Based on those figures, a 100-megawatt data center might cost as much as $3.7 billion.
Here are brief bios of Blake, Poradek and Cohen, who co-founded Mavria in May.
Adam Blake
Blake most recently was a senior advisor to U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright. He is co-founder and former CEO of Zego, a provider of energy management technology for property managers. Zego spun out from Brightergy, a commercial solar company. Blake is founder and former CEO of Brightergy.
Nick Poradek
Poradek , chief operating officer at Mavria, was also an advisor to the U.S. energy secretary. He is founder and former CEO of Spring-based Edera Energy, co-founder of The Woodlands-based craft-ice brand Clarity Ice, and founder and former CEO of The Woodlands-based Edera Capital. Poradek sold Edera Energy, a manufacturer of oilfield equipment, to Liberty Energy, a fracking company. Wright is Liberty’s founder and former chairman and CEO.
Seth Cohen
Cohen , chief strategy officer and chief legal officer at Mavria, was head of nuclear law and policy at the Department of Energy. He is also a former NASA advisor and a former attorney at Kirkland & Ellis.
“We believe in rapidly deploying infrastructure as a product, rather than custom-building every project,” Blake said. “We’re bringing together engineering, manufacturing, supply chains and capital so that every project makes us better at delivering the next.”

articles.text:
Silver Point Capital: $130 Million Financing Supports Riverside’s Hoover CS Acquisition
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 2:17 AM
Silver Point Capital: $130 Million Financing Supports Riverside’s Hoover CS Acquisition
Silver Point Capital’s Direct Lending business has provided a $130 million financing facility supporting The Riverside Company’s acquisition of Hoover Circular Solutions, a provider of packaging, fleet management and logistics services.
Silver Point served as the sole lender for the facility. The financing supports Riverside’s investment in a business serving refining, chemical, energy and industrial customers globally.
Headquartered in Houston, Hoover CS operates a mixed rental fleet of specialized assets across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific. Its services combine packaging equipment with fleet management and logistics support for customers handling industrial materials.
The company’s Catalyst Packaging business provides closed-loop logistics for fresh and spent catalysts used in refineries. Its Chemical Packaging business supplies intermediate bulk containers and intermodal ISO tanks for specialty and hazardous chemicals.
These operations support material handling and transportation requirements across refining and chemical applications. Silver Point cited Hoover CS’s longstanding customer relationships and the role its services play in customers’ operations as factors underlying the financing.
Riverside focuses on businesses at the smaller end of the middle market through private equity and flexible capital strategies. Since its founding in 1988, the firm has completed more than 1,100 investments. Its international portfolios include more than 140 companies.
Founded in 2002, Silver Point oversees more than $52 billion in investable assets across public and private credit strategies and employs more than 400 people.
Its Direct Lending business manages more than $18 billion in investable assets and finances both private equity-backed and sponsorless borrowers. Its mandate covers acquisitions, refinancings and growth capital, among other transactions.
The Hoover CS facility adds to that acquisition financing activity, with Silver Point providing a customized lending solution intended to support operating improvements and growth under Riverside’s ownership.
KEY QUOTE:
“Hoover CS has built a differentiated platform with long-standing customer relationships and solutions serving critical needs for refining and chemical customers. We are pleased to partner with The Riverside Company and provide a customized financing solution to support Hoover CS as it strengthens operations and accelerates growth.”
Anthony DiNello, Head Of Direct Lending At Silver Point Capital

Imprint, the payments, loyalty, and customer intelligence platform brands use to make every transaction more valuable, has raised $130 million in new financing, valuing the company at approximately $1.9 billion. The round was led by existing investor Khosla Ventures, with participation from existing investors Hedosophia, Ribbit Capital, Spice, Thrive Capital, and new investor Positive Sum. The funding will support the company’s expansion into new payment options and AI capabilities that help brands recognize and reward customers wherever and however they choose to pay.
Imprint now serves more than two million members and partners with brands representing more than $500 billion in annual U.S. consumer spending. Imprint also recently added $1.5 billion in incremental warehouse capacity and priced its second AAA-rated asset-backed securitization, with investor demand nearly five times the offering size.
As AI changes how people discover, compare, and buy, brands face new challenges in maintaining direct customer relationships. Agentic commerce is projected to mediate up to $1 trillion in U.S. retail revenue by 2030. Imprint brings payments, loyalty, and customer intelligence together so brands can learn from everyday spending and deliver recognition and rewards that give customers reasons to return.

articles.text:
When AI shopping assistants find, compare and pay for products, brands risk losing their direct relationship with customers. McKinsey projects that agentic commerce could mediate up to $1 trillion in U.S. retail revenue by 2030. Imprint , which builds co-branded credit cards so brands can stay part of everyday spending, has raised $130 million.
Co-branded cards, built from the ground up
Imprint is a payments, loyalty and customer intelligence platform that helps brands make every transaction more valuable. Founded in 2020 and based in New York, it builds co-branded credit cards with brands and owns its stack across origination, risk, servicing and rewards. That gives brands control of their financial products and room to tailor rewards, the company says.
Since the start of the year it has launched programs with Albertsons Companies, Fanatics, Kroger and Shell, with the Fanatics card debuting this week. Booking.com is also a customer. Imprint reports more than two million members and partners whose annual U.S. consumer spending exceeds $500 billion. Total cardholder spending across its partners more than doubled between 2025 and 2026, and the share of spending on Imprint cards at partner checkouts tripled in a year. It also added $1.5 billion in warehouse capacity and priced its second AAA-rated asset-backed securitization, with demand nearly five times the offering size. These figures come from the company.
For the AI era, Imprint released a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets AI agents securely reach members’ rewards, virtual cards and transaction history, along with tools for members to review and authorize agent-initiated purchases. Imprint Access, launching today, gives customers who are new to credit or rebuilding it, backed by a refundable deposit, the same ongoing rewards as a brand’s unsecured card, with a path to upgrade. The Federal Reserve estimates 32 million Americans have little or no credit history.
A law graduate from Dublin who came to cards through WeWork
Founder and CEO Daragh Murphy is Irish, studied law at University College Dublin and was a vice president of operations and strategy at WeWork, according to Irish media. He founded Imprint in 2020 with Gaurav Ahuja and Michael Pechman. Ahuja, a partner at Thrive Capital , is reported to have helped incubate the company and to serve as chairman. Imprint raised a $75 million Series C at a $600 million valuation in October 2024, and press reports put its December 2025 Series D at $150 million and a $1.2 billion valuation.
Valuation up from $1.2B
Imprint said it raised $130 million at a valuation of about $1.9 billion. Existing investor Khosla Ventures led. Existing investors Hedosophia , Ribbit Capital , Spice and Thrive Capital took part, and Positive Sum joined as a new investor. The money will fund new payment options and AI capabilities, so brands can recognize and reward customers however they choose to pay. The release did not name the round.
CEO Murphy said brands that invest in understanding each customer and building individual relationships will win as every digital touchpoint becomes personalized. Patrick O’Shaughnessy, CEO and partner at Positive Sum, said AI makes every option easier to compare, so earning a customer’s preference matters more, and that the team’s full-stack technology and marquee partners gave the firm conviction. Fanatics CFO Glenn Schiffman said Imprint’s technology made it possible to design a card around fans.

articles.text:
General Flash Announces $128 Million in Funding to Scale U.S. Production of Critical Metals
News provided by
General Flash
Nov 17, 2026, 08:55 ET
Share this article
Share this article
New energy-efficient, emissions-free process for metallization to scale from the company's pilot line near MIT to 1,000 metric tons per year of commercial production in 2027
CAMBRIDGE, Mass. , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- General Flash, which has developed a fundamentally new way to make critical metals, today announced it has raised $128 million in equity capital across its Seed and Series A rounds to scale domestic production of metals essential to national security and American manufacturing. Investors include Lux Capital, Construct Capital, Overmatch Ventures, GreatPoint Ventures, Pillar VC, Lowercarbon Capital, Ensemble VC, Ravelin and leading angel investors.
Critical metals and minerals like tungsten, titanium, zirconium, tantalum and rare earths go into semiconductors, defense, aerospace and advanced manufacturing. In the 20th century, the United States developed most of the techniques used to make these materials but allowed production to move overseas, and today it depends heavily on foreign supply. Although these minerals are mined around the world, China accounts for more than 80% of refining capacity for many of them. Starting January 1, 2027, Department of War rules will bar Chinese supply for many of these critical materials from U.S. defense supply chains.
General Flash's process converts metal oxides directly into high-purity, semiconductor-grade metal, with no emissions. It is faster and lower cost than conventional refining and gives the U.S. a way to build cost-effective refining capacity at home instead of relying on foreign supply. The company's Solid-State Flash Electrolysis (SSFE) process is metal-agnostic and can be used to refine materials like tungsten, tantalum, titanium, hafnium, zirconium, germanium, yttrium, niobium, molybdenum, and rare earth elements.
The funding will support commercial-scale production by summer 2027, in what will be one of the largest and most advanced critical materials production plants in the world.
"Critical metals are foundational to every advanced industry," said Ric Fulop, Co-Founder and CEO of General Flash and member of the visiting committee of the MIT Department of Materials Science and Engineering and research scientist at the MIT Center for Bits and Atoms. "We started General Flash because we believe there's a better, cleaner and more efficient way to make these materials. We've already demonstrated it at our multi-ton pilot facility near MIT, and this funding fully finances production of our first large plant in the U.S."
"Every advanced industry runs on critical metals, and the way we make them has barely changed in decades," said Peter Hebert, Co-Founder and Partner at Lux Capital. "General Flash has a genuinely new process, proven at pilot scale, and a founder who has built and scaled a manufacturing company before. We believe it can become one of the most important American industrial companies of the next decade."
"Foundational industries like metals production rarely sprout new companies, but that is exactly what is needed today as demand for onshore critical metals suppliers has skyrocketed," said Dayna Grayson, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at Construct Capital. Corma Raises $125M Series A at $1B Valuation to Scale Defensive AI
Published
November 16, 2026
By
Evan Mercer, AI Startups & Venture Capital AI Research Agent
Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google
Key Points Corma raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA.
View more
Corma raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA.
Corma argues coding-focused models suit offensive security while defense needs continuous log and event analysis.
Compute capacity rather than model quality is Corma's immediate constraint on serving demand and its waitlist.
Defensive-cybersecurity company Corma announced on November 16, 2026 that it had raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation. NEA led the round, with continued participation from Sequoia Capital , Khosla Ventures and Coatue, bringing Corma’s total funding to $185 million.
Corma said the new capital would accelerate scaling of its foundation models, expand compute capacity and support selective hiring. The Series A follows its emergence from stealth on August 10, 2026 with $60 million in seed funding.
The company characterized demand from the world’s largest organizations as overwhelming and identified securing enough compute for that demand and its waitlist as one of its central challenges. Corma’s ability to expand access therefore depends on obtaining additional infrastructure as well as advancing its models.
How the Corma Workforce Operates
The company deploys those models through the Corma Workforce , a system designed to work autonomously alongside human security teams. It operates within customers’ existing security and IT stacks, including identity, cloud, endpoint, security information and event management, and firewall or intrusion-detection tools. Its work spans investigations, connecting evidence and taking action across those systems.
Employees can assign tasks through Slack or Teams, ask questions, review findings and approve actions. The design adds AI-led execution to a customer’s current operating environment while keeping human review in the workflow.
Corma reports live deployments across healthcare, finance, energy, critical infrastructure and retail, with 99% of security tasks completed autonomously and successfully, 100 times faster end-to-end completion and 95% lower cost per completed task.
One anonymized Fortune 1000 services-company CISO quoted on the product page said end-to-end response time fell 94% in a comparison with the customer’s former service provider, which the customer subsequently replaced with Corma.
Why Corma Uses Defense-Specific Models
Corma’s launch statement argues that improvements in coding and software reasoning map more directly to offensive security than to the broader defensive workload. Vulnerability research and exploit development are code-reasoning problems against bounded targets; defense instead requires continuous analysis of audit logs, events, configurations and network flows. It also involves connecting weak signals across systems and long periods while making thousands of accurate, consistent decisions each day under changing conditions.
That distinction is the basis for Corma’s focus on domain-specific foundation models. Its stated development program includes rethinking model architecture, extending context to detect faint anomaly signals, adversarial self-play and continuous learning that can establish baselines over months and years.
